newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom row may not spark change - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom row may not spark change - analysts.

text.p: A fiery debate over who should control Russian gas monopoly Gazprom has turned up the heat on the world's biggest gas company, but the verbal sparks may not lead to fundamental reform of the firm, analysts said Friday.
They said restructuring the industrial behemoth was likely to be superficial with no fundamental shakeup at the monopoly.
"The latest statements by the company and the government will not change the company's make-up," said Ivan Mazalov, oil and gas specialist at CentreInvest Securities in Moscow.

A war of words over the nature and pace of restructuring Gazprom intensified on Thursday when privatisation minister Alfred Kokh threatened to take back control of a 35 percent Gazprom stake managed by the company's highest official.

The comments came after Gazprom chief executive officer Rem Vyakhirev told conservative parliamentarians that foreign energy firms were working through the government to push structural changes at the company.
Analysts said the verbal volleys would not translate into cataclysmic changes soon at Gazprom.
"For the next year or two, I would expect the status quo at Gazprom to continue," said Stuart Amor, oil and gas analyst at CS First Boston in London.

Some analysts interpreted Vyakhirev's hardline speech as an attempt to regain control of the gas giant now that Prime Minister Victor Chernomyrdin, former Gazprom head, has seemed to be taking a back seat in the newly-formed government.

"Vyakhirev may be under pressure to consolidate his political base, as...Chernomyrdin assumes a lower-key role in the Cabinet, and President (Boris) Yeltsin appears to give more support to the aggressively pro-reform first deputy premiers," Renaissance Capital bank said in a commentary.

The likely appointment of former Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov, also a former Gazprom employee, to the post of deputy chairman of Gazprom's board, was not expected to have a major impact on the way the company was run.
"I would expect him to fit into the mould," Amor said.

Yeltsin has handed the task of restructuring Russia's gas and two other natural monopolies -- railways and electricity -- to dynamic reformist Boris Nemtsov, made First Deputy Prime Minister last month.
Nemtsov has said the government should increase its role both in state power utility Unified Energy System (UES) and in Gazprom.
"Nemtsov and Anatoly Chubais (also First Deputy Prime Minister) may be successful in introducing new management to Unified, but my guess would be that Gazprom is just too powerful," Amor said.
A few analysts say Gazprom may eventually be split into three units -- output, transport and marketing -- but they say such major restructuring would probably take years.
The separate units could well remain 100-percent owned by the company -- raising doubts over how much impact a split would have on efficiency and price transparency.
Gazprom controls around one third of the world's gas reserves and is a major exporter to Western Europe.
Russia plans to produce 614 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas in 1997, from 601 billion in 1996. Gazprom accounted for 94 percent of the total.
Despite its huge production and export base, Gazprom is ensnared in a web of nonpayments and other debts.
It owed around 15 trillion roubles ($2.6 billion) in overdue taxes at the end of last year, but was owed over three times that amount by customers which had not paid for supplies.
